title: Approved contrast doses limit microbubble functional ultrasound of human cortex to 0.5–1 mm voxels per session even with perfect bubble counting, in a Poisson model checked on mouse ULM data
abstract: Contrast-based functional ultrasound cannot map human cortical activity at the microscopic scale of its vessel images: the number of microbubbles that the drug labels permit sets a floor of about 0.5-1 mm on the side of a voxel that can show a typical blood-flow response in one session, even if every bubble is counted. This matters because transcranial functional ultrasound localization microscopy (fULM; imaging that finds single injected microbubbles and maps vessels at about 25 um) is planned as a noninvasive high-resolution alternative to fMRI. We treat each bubble that enters a voxel as one count of a Poisson process. The US labels fix the largest bubble exposure (concentration x time) of one session: for Definity, about 3700 bubble passages per mm^3 of cortex. For a 30% flow increase, detection index 3 and 0.6 mL/g/min blood flow, an ideal counter needs a voxel side of 0.50 mm per session at the label maximum (0.62 mm, 5-95% range 0.48-0.81, when the real concentration is 0.3-1 times the label value) and about 2 mm in one 2-s trial. A (25 um)^3 parenchymal voxel needs about 10^6 trials, and one capillary needs about 2 h of stimulus, 45 times more than one dose permits. If only 10% or 1% of bubbles are detected, the session voxel grows to 1.3 or 2.9 mm. Scenarios with localizer saturation (a localizer separates only a few bubbles per point-spread volume) give 6.5 mm in-plane voxels per session for a 2-D probe through the temporal window, and no single-trial detection. Contrast-free power Doppler is statistically better than even the ideal counter if its blood-to-noise ratio per resolution cell is above -3.5 to +9 dB. In public mouse ULM acquisitions (ULMShare; 10 at 15.6 MHz), voxel counts were near Poisson below 1 s (Fano factor 0.93-1.3), and a Poisson power formula predicted semi-synthetic detection rates within 0.04. Detected counts did not follow injected dose (slope 0.10), but this comparison is confounded and does not measure a saturation density. Limits: detection efficiency, saturation density and visible blood fraction are not measured in humans, so the realistic-array numbers are scenarios; clutter, motion and skull heating are not modelled and can only make times longer.
